question: A 65-year-old man reports that food sticks immediately after swallowing, he frequently coughs and splutters, and has nasal regurgitation. Which type of dysphagia does this pattern most suggest?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Peptic stricture causes oesophageal dysphagia — food sticks in the mid-chest after a delay, not immediately on swallowing. Coughing and nasal regurgitation point to the oropharyngeal phase.

answers.text: Oropharyngeal dysphagia due to a neuromuscular disorder

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Immediate post-swallow sticking, coughing/aspiration, and nasal regurgitation are hallmarks of oropharyngeal (transfer) dysphagia, most often neuromuscular in origin (e.g., bulbar palsy, Parkinson disease).
Achalasia causes progressive dysphagia to both solids and liquids, with food sticking in the lower chest — not immediate transfer failure with aspiration and nasal regurgitation.
Functional dysphagia is a diagnosis of exclusion. The objective signs here — nasal regurgitation, coughing, immediate onset — indicate true oropharyngeal phase failure, not functional aetiology.

overallFeedback.feedback: Recall the clinical pearl: solid-only dysphagia = mechanical obstruction; immediate symptoms + aspiration/regurgitation = oropharyngeal/neuromuscular. Review the Clinical Presentation section.
Well done. Oropharyngeal dysphagia presents with transfer failure — immediate post-swallow symptoms, aspiration, and nasal regurgitation — distinguishing it clearly from oesophageal dysphagia.
